claims.text: An integrated pulsed-laser, DSC, and synchrotron X-ray method can accurately determine melting temperatures across a wide range of HEAs.
The integrated method can accurately determine HEA enthalpies of fusion.
The integrated method can accurately determine HEA entropies of fusion.
The integrated method can accurately determine volume changes at melting.
The measurements enable extraction of derived liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
The proposed integrated method is efficient across a broad HEA composition space.
Solid-solution HEAs made by conventional melting or powder-based processing can provide homogeneous starting microstructures.
Laser-based melting or processing can be applied to an HEA in an inert atmosphere.
DSC and synchrotron X-ray imaging can be operated simultaneously during rapid pulsed laser melting.
Transient liquid microstructure and volume expansion during rapid melting can be captured by synchrotron imaging and correlated with calorimetric signals.
Latent heat produced during rapid laser melting can be quantitatively detected by DSC.
Volumetric expansion during rapid laser melting can be quantitatively imaged in real time.
Correlating calorimetric and imaging signals permits extraction of energetic and volume-based thermodynamic properties.
Rapid dynamic heating mitigates prolonged diffusion and elemental segregation that can obscure conventional DSC melting transitions.
Melting temperatures can be resolved with an uncertainty of ±5 °C.
Fusion enthalpies can be determined within ±5% relative error.
Volume changes at melting can be captured with approximately ±2–3% resolution.
Conventional DSC or static calorimetry often has reduced resolution because of slow heating and phase segregation.
Very high melting points, severe segregation kinetics, undercooling, and laser-induced thermal gradients can limit the method or bias equilibrium-property measurements.
Consistent deviations greater than approximately 10% or beyond the specified resolution limits relative to independent conventional measurements would falsify the proposed accuracy.
